title: A venture capital scheme has 48 investors and wishes to admit 4 more,
topic_name: Alternative Investment Funds – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: A venture capital scheme has 48 investors and wishes to admit 4 more, each investing USD 300,000. The compliance officer should identify that:
option_a: The additional investors are permissible because each exceeds the USD 250,000 minimum
option_b: The scheme may admit them only after converting into a restricted scheme structure
option_c: The ceiling applies to accredited investors only, so the admissions are unaffected
option_d: Admitting all four would breach the fifty-investor ceiling applicable to VC schemes

options.text: The additional investors are permissible because each exceeds the USD 250,000 minimum
The scheme may admit them only after converting into a restricted scheme structure
The ceiling applies to accredited investors only, so the admissions are unaffected
Admitting all four would breach the fifty-investor ceiling applicable to VC schemes

explanation: The ticket size is satisfied, but the investor ceiling for a VC scheme is fifty. Admitting four more would take the scheme to fifty-two. Meeting one condition does not cure a breach of another — the classic error in scheme structuring.

title: A VC scheme's placement memorandum is silent on leverage, but the FME
topic_name: Alternative Investment Funds – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: A VC scheme's placement memorandum is silent on leverage, but the FME wishes to borrow short-term to bridge a drawdown. The correct position is that borrowing:
option_a: Requires the maximum leverage and its calculation methodology to be disclosed in the PPM
option_b: Is prohibited outright, since venture capital schemes may never employ leverage
option_c: Is permitted, because bridge borrowing against committed capital is always excluded
option_d: Requires the prior approval of the Authority for each individual borrowing transaction

options.text: Requires the maximum leverage and its calculation methodology to be disclosed in the PPM
Is prohibited outright, since venture capital schemes may never employ leverage
Is permitted, because bridge borrowing against committed capital is always excluded
Requires the prior approval of the Authority for each individual borrowing transaction

explanation: Leverage is permitted subject to conditions, including disclosure of the maximum leverage and the methodology for calculating it in the placement memorandum. A PPM silent on the point cannot support the borrowing until it is amended.

title: A VC scheme values its portfolio through the FME's own internal commit
topic_name: Alternative Investment Funds – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: A VC scheme values its portfolio through the FME's own internal committee and computes NAV once a year. Which element is defective?
option_a: Neither — annual NAV and internal valuation are both permitted for VC schemes
option_b: The valuation, because it must be carried out by an independent service provider
option_c: The NAV frequency, because venture capital schemes require quarterly computation
option_d: Both, because VC schemes must value monthly and appoint an external administrator

options.text: Neither — annual NAV and internal valuation are both permitted for VC schemes
The valuation, because it must be carried out by an independent service provider
The NAV frequency, because venture capital schemes require quarterly computation
Both, because VC schemes must value monthly and appoint an external administrator

explanation: Annual NAV is permitted for a VC scheme provided the methodology is documented. Valuation, however, must be performed by an independent service provider — a fund administrator, custodian, registered CRA or IBBI-registered valuer. An internal committee does not satisfy that.

title: VC Minimum Investment — Above or At Least?
topic_name: Alternative Investment Funds – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: Under the current 2025 regulations, a non-accredited investor may invest in a Venture Capital scheme by investing:
option_a: Above USD 250,000 — strictly more than the threshold, as under the 2022 regulations
option_b: At least USD 150,000
option_c: Any amount, if the scheme has fewer than 50 investors
option_d: At least USD 250,000 — exactly USD 250,000 qualifies

options.text: Above USD 250,000 — strictly more than the threshold, as under the 2022 regulations
At least USD 150,000
Any amount, if the scheme has fewer than 50 investors
At least USD 250,000 — exactly USD 250,000 qualifies

explanation: 2025 requires "at least USD 250,000", so exactly USD 250,000 qualifies; 2022's "above USD 250,000" excluded it. Employees/directors/designated partners: minimum USD 60,000. USD 150,000 is the lower application size that pushes a scheme into the restricted route.

title: VC Corpus — Floor and Ceiling
topic_name: Alternative Investment Funds – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: A Venture Capital scheme's corpus must be:
option_a: At least USD 3 Million and not exceeding USD 200 Million
option_b: At least USD 1 Million with no ceiling
option_c: At least USD 5 Million and not exceeding USD 100 Million
option_d: At least USD 3 Million with no ceiling

options.text: At least USD 3 Million and not exceeding USD 200 Million
At least USD 1 Million with no ceiling
At least USD 5 Million and not exceeding USD 100 Million
At least USD 3 Million with no ceiling

explanation: Reg. 23(1) sets both ends: USD 3M minimum, USD 200M maximum. VC is the only mainstream scheme type with a corpus ceiling — target more and you must use the restricted-scheme route.

title: The 80/10 Rule
topic_name: Alternative Investment Funds – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: A Venture Capital scheme must invest at least 80% of its corpus in:
option_a: Securities listed on a recognised stock exchange in the IFSC or in any foreign jurisdiction
option_b: Investee companies incorporated not more than ten (10) years ago, or other schemes meeting that requirement
option_c: Investee companies incorporated not more than five (5) years ago, or other schemes meeting that test
option_d: Government securities, money market instruments and other cash equivalents held in the IFSC

options.text: Securities listed on a recognised stock exchange in the IFSC or in any foreign jurisdiction
Investee companies incorporated not more than ten (10) years ago, or other schemes meeting that requirement
Investee companies incorporated not more than five (5) years ago, or other schemes meeting that test
Government securities, money market instruments and other cash equivalents held in the IFSC

explanation: Reg. 23(3): ≥80% of corpus into companies within 10 years of incorporation — the provision that keeps "venture capital" venture. Feeder investment into other compliant schemes also counts.

title: Skin in the Game — Smaller VC Schemes
topic_name: Alternative Investment Funds – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: For a VC scheme with targeted corpus up to USD 30 Million, the FME or its associate must invest:
option_a: At least 5% and not more than 10% of the targeted corpus
option_b: A flat USD 750,000
option_c: At least 2.5% and not more than 10% of the targeted corpus
option_d: At least 1% with no upper limit

options.text: At least 5% and not more than 10% of the targeted corpus
A flat USD 750,000
At least 2.5% and not more than 10% of the targeted corpus
At least 1% with no upper limit

explanation: Reg. 28(1)(a): 2.5%–10% band for schemes up to USD 30M targeted corpus. The floor aligns manager incentives; the cap prevents the FME dominating its own fund.

title: Skin in the Game — Larger VC Schemes
topic_name: Alternative Investment Funds – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: For a VC scheme with targeted corpus above USD 30 Million, the FME/associate contribution is:
option_a: At least 2.5% of the targeted corpus, whatever the size
option_b: At least USD 1,500,000, not exceeding 10%
option_c: Waived entirely above USD 30 Million
option_d: At least USD 750,000, not exceeding 10% of the targeted corpus

options.text: At least 2.5% of the targeted corpus, whatever the size
At least USD 1,500,000, not exceeding 10%
Waived entirely above USD 30 Million
At least USD 750,000, not exceeding 10% of the targeted corpus

explanation: Above USD 30M the floor becomes absolute: USD 750,000 (the 2.5%-of-30M figure frozen), capped at 10%. The contribution is not mandatory for schemes relocated to IFSC from outside India.

title: Investing in Your Own Associate
topic_name: Alternative Investment Funds – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: A VC scheme may invest in an associate of the FME:
option_a: Subject to prior approval of 75% of investors in the scheme by value
option_b: Freely, if disclosed in the placement memorandum
option_c: Never — associate investments are prohibited
option_d: With prior approval of a simple majority of investors by number

options.text: Subject to prior approval of 75% of investors in the scheme by value
Freely, if disclosed in the placement memorandum
Never — associate investments are prohibited
With prior approval of a simple majority of investors by number

explanation: Reg. 23(2): associate investments need prior approval of 75% of investors by value — the recurring supermajority standard for conflicted transactions across the regulations.

title: VC NAV Frequency
topic_name: Alternative Investment Funds – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: The FME must compute the NAV of each Venture Capital scheme:
option_a: Daily, in line with the practice followed for retail schemes
option_b: At least on an annual basis, with fully documented methodology
option_c: Monthly, and disclosed to investors within ten working days
option_d: Only at the time of winding up the scheme and its final distribution

options.text: Daily, in line with the practice followed for retail schemes
At least on an annual basis, with fully documented methodology
Monthly, and disclosed to investors within ten working days
Only at the time of winding up the scheme and its final distribution

explanation: Reg. 27: annual minimum, with the calculation procedure documented, regularly verified and amended where needed. Illiquid venture portfolios don't warrant daily NAVs — but they do demand methodological discipline.

title: Who May Value the Assets
topic_name: Alternative Investment Funds – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: The assets of a VC scheme must be valued by an independent service provider, which may be:
option_a: Only a chartered accountant holding a certificate of practice, appointed and rotated by the FME periodically
option_b: The FME's own internal valuation committee, provided that it excludes the scheme's own fund managers
option_c: A fund administrator, a custodian, a credit rating agency registered with the Authority, or an IBBI-registered valuer
option_d: Any merchant banker registered with a securities regulator in India or in a comparable foreign jurisdiction

options.text: Only a chartered accountant holding a certificate of practice, appointed and rotated by the FME periodically
The FME's own internal valuation committee, provided that it excludes the scheme's own fund managers
A fund administrator, a custodian, a credit rating agency registered with the Authority, or an IBBI-registered valuer
Any merchant banker registered with a securities regulator in India or in a comparable foreign jurisdiction

explanation: Reg. 26(2) lists the eligible independents: fund administrator, custodian, Authority-registered CRA, IBBI-registered valuer, or others as specified. Valuation norms themselves sit in the Sixth Schedule.

title: An open-ended restricted scheme has raised USD 2.4 Million and wishes
topic_name: Alternative Investment Funds – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: An open-ended restricted scheme has raised USD 2.4 Million and wishes to take a 15% position in an unlisted company. The compliance officer should advise that:
option_a: The investment is permitted, since 15% is comfortably within the 25% unlisted cap
option_b: The investment is permitted only if the unlisted company is incorporated in the IFSC
option_c: The investment must wait until the scheme achieves the USD 3 Million minimum corpus
option_d: The scheme cannot invest in unlisted securities at all while it remains open-ended

options.text: The investment is permitted, since 15% is comfortably within the 25% unlisted cap
The investment is permitted only if the unlisted company is incorporated in the IFSC
The investment must wait until the scheme achieves the USD 3 Million minimum corpus
The scheme cannot invest in unlisted securities at all while it remains open-ended

explanation: The 25% cap is satisfied, but the second proviso to Reg. 35(1) inserted in 2026 bars unlisted investment altogether until the scheme achieves the USD 3 Million minimum corpus. Two separate conditions apply and both must be met.

title: A restricted scheme proposes to buy an asset from an investor holding
topic_name: Alternative Investment Funds – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: A restricted scheme proposes to buy an asset from an investor holding 55% of its commitments. Approval is obtained from 78% of investors by value, counting that investor's vote. The position is that:
option_a: The approval is valid, since the 75% threshold by value has clearly been exceeded
option_b: The approval is invalid, since such transactions require unanimous investor consent
option_c: The approval is valid, provided the transaction is disclosed in the next annual report
option_d: The approval is invalid, since the interested investor's votes must be excluded

options.text: The approval is valid, since the 75% threshold by value has clearly been exceeded
The approval is invalid, since such transactions require unanimous investor consent
The approval is valid, provided the transaction is disclosed in the next annual report
The approval is invalid, since the interested investor's votes must be excluded

explanation: Reg. 35(4) requires 75% approval by value excluding the votes of the investor concerned. Counting the 55% investor's own vote inflates the tally — the exclusion is precisely what makes the safeguard meaningful.

title: A close-ended restricted scheme with a targeted corpus of USD 40 Milli
topic_name: Alternative Investment Funds – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: A close-ended restricted scheme with a targeted corpus of USD 40 Million proposes an FME contribution of USD 900,000. The compliance officer should identify that this:
option_a: Satisfies the floor, since USD 750,000 is the applicable minimum for close-ended schemes
option_b: Falls short, because the floor for a corpus above USD 30 Million is USD 1,500,000
option_c: Exceeds the ceiling, because contribution is capped at 2.5% of the targeted corpus
option_d: Satisfies the floor, provided the balance is contributed before the scheme's first close

options.text: Satisfies the floor, since USD 750,000 is the applicable minimum for close-ended schemes
Falls short, because the floor for a corpus above USD 30 Million is USD 1,500,000
Exceeds the ceiling, because contribution is capped at 2.5% of the targeted corpus
Satisfies the floor, provided the balance is contributed before the scheme's first close

explanation: For close-ended restricted schemes the floor is 2.5% of targeted corpus or USD 750,000, whichever is lower. The USD 1,500,000 figure belongs to the open-ended regime under Reg. 40(b). Confusing the two floors is the common error.

title: Restricted Scheme Investor Cap
topic_name: Alternative Investment Funds – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: A restricted scheme may have at most:
option_a: Fifty (50) investors, matching the venture capital scheme ceiling
option_b: Two hundred (200) investors, in line with the private placement limit
option_c: One thousand (1000) investors, or such number as the Authority specifies
option_d: No limit at all, provided each meets the minimum investment threshold

options.text: Fifty (50) investors, matching the venture capital scheme ceiling
Two hundred (200) investors, in line with the private placement limit
One thousand (1000) investors, or such number as the Authority specifies
No limit at all, provided each meets the minimum investment threshold

explanation: Reg. 32(1): 1000-investor ceiling (subject to Authority variation). The 50-investor cap belongs to VC schemes; retail schemes have no ceiling at all.

title: Which Restricted Schemes Can Be Open-Ended
topic_name: Alternative Investment Funds – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: Among restricted schemes filed as Category I, II and III AIFs, open-ended structure is available to:
option_a: All three categories, at the option of the fund management entity
option_b: Category I and II schemes only, since Category III must be close-ended
option_c: None — every restricted scheme must be filed as a close-ended scheme
option_d: Category III schemes only — Category I and II must be close-ended

options.text: All three categories, at the option of the fund management entity
Category I and II schemes only, since Category III must be close-ended
None — every restricted scheme must be filed as a close-ended scheme
Category III schemes only — Category I and II must be close-ended

explanation: Reg. 30(2): schemes under clauses (a) and (c) — the Cat I and Cat II routes — file close-ended; only clause (b) schemes (Cat III) may file open- or close-ended.

title: Open-Ended Commencement Ladder
topic_name: Alternative Investment Funds – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: An open-ended restricted scheme may commence investment activities upon raising:
option_a: USD 1 Million, achieving the USD 3 Million minimum corpus within 12 months of the taken-on-record communication
option_b: USD 3 Million in full and upfront, before any investment activity of the scheme may commence
option_c: USD 500,000, with no further corpus milestone applying to the scheme thereafter at all
option_d: USD 2 Million, achieving the USD 3 Million minimum corpus within six months of the launch date

options.text: USD 1 Million, achieving the USD 3 Million minimum corpus within 12 months of the taken-on-record communication
USD 3 Million in full and upfront, before any investment activity of the scheme may commence
USD 500,000, with no further corpus milestone applying to the scheme thereafter at all
USD 2 Million, achieving the USD 3 Million minimum corpus within six months of the launch date

explanation: The two-step ladder: start at USD 1M, reach USD 3M within 12 months. Post the 2026 Amendment, unlisted securities remain off-limits until USD 3M is achieved.

title: Skin in the Game — Close-Ended
topic_name: Alternative Investment Funds – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: For a close-ended restricted scheme with targeted corpus up to USD 30 Million, the FME/associate must invest:
option_a: At least 5% and not more than 10%
option_b: At least 2.5% and not more than 10% of the targeted corpus
option_c: At least USD 1,500,000
option_d: Nothing — skin in the game applies only to VC schemes

options.text: At least 5% and not more than 10%
At least 2.5% and not more than 10% of the targeted corpus
At least USD 1,500,000
Nothing — skin in the game applies only to VC schemes

explanation: Reg. 40(a): close-ended restricted schemes mirror the VC bands — 2.5%–10% up to USD 30M; ≥USD 750,000 (≤10%) above it.

title: Skin in the Game — Open-Ended
topic_name: Alternative Investment Funds – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: For an open-ended restricted scheme, the FME/associate contribution floor is:
option_a: 2.5% of targeted corpus, or USD 750,000 — the same floor as for close-ended schemes
option_b: A flat 1% of assets under management of the scheme, measured at each year end
option_c: 5% of targeted corpus (below USD 30M), or USD 1,500,000 (above USD 30M) — both capped at 10%
option_d: Nil, since open-ended schemes already offer redemption liquidity to investors

options.text: 2.5% of targeted corpus, or USD 750,000 — the same floor as for close-ended schemes
A flat 1% of assets under management of the scheme, measured at each year end
5% of targeted corpus (below USD 30M), or USD 1,500,000 (above USD 30M) — both capped at 10%
Nil, since open-ended schemes already offer redemption liquidity to investors

explanation: Reg. 40(b): open-ended schemes carry double the close-ended floors — 5% / USD 1.5M — reflecting the higher risk manager-investor misalignment poses when investors can redeem.

title: Trading With Associates
topic_name: Alternative Investment Funds – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: A restricted scheme may buy or sell securities from associates, other schemes of the FME, or an investor committed to 50%+ of the corpus:
option_a: Freely, provided that the transaction is disclosed to the investors after it has been completed
option_b: Never, under any circumstances, whatever approval the investors may be willing to give
option_c: With the prior approval of a simple majority of investors, counting all investors alike
option_d: Only with prior approval of 75% of investors by value — excluding the votes of the 50%+ committed investor

options.text: Freely, provided that the transaction is disclosed to the investors after it has been completed
Never, under any circumstances, whatever approval the investors may be willing to give
With the prior approval of a simple majority of investors, counting all investors alike
Only with prior approval of 75% of investors by value — excluding the votes of the 50%+ committed investor

explanation: Reg. 35(4): conflicted trades need the 75%-by-value supermajority, and the conflicted mega-investor is excluded from the vote — approval must come from the unconflicted.

title: Segregated Portfolio Co-Investment
topic_name: Alternative Investment Funds – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: When a restricted scheme co-invests through a segregated portfolio (separate unit class), the segregated portfolio's investment terms must be:
option_a: In no circumstances more favourable than those offered to the common portfolio
option_b: Identical in every respect to the terms offered to the common portfolio
option_c: More favourable, so as to compensate co-investors for the concentration risk
option_d: Left entirely to commercial negotiation between the FME and the co-investors

options.text: In no circumstances more favourable than those offered to the common portfolio
Identical in every respect to the terms offered to the common portfolio
More favourable, so as to compensate co-investors for the concentration risk
Left entirely to commercial negotiation between the FME and the co-investors

explanation: Reg. 41(2)(a): co-investors may get access, but never better terms than the main pool — protecting common-portfolio investors from structural subordination. Disclosure in the PPM is also mandatory.

title: Leverage Through the Co-Investment SPV
topic_name: Alternative Investment Funds – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: An SPV used by a restricted scheme for co-investment may undertake leverage:
option_a: Never — SPVs must be unleveraged
option_b: As disclosed in the placement memorandum
option_c: Up to 2x NAV as a hard cap
option_d: Only with case-by-case IFSCA approval

options.text: Never — SPVs must be unleveraged
As disclosed in the placement memorandum
Up to 2x NAV as a hard cap
Only with case-by-case IFSCA approval

explanation: Reg. 41(3): SPV leverage is a disclosure matter — permitted to the extent the PPM discloses it. The framework consistently prefers disclosed flexibility over hard caps for sophisticated-investor products.

title: An SSF placement memorandum expired last week without the minimum corp
topic_name: Alternative Investment Funds – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: An SSF placement memorandum expired last week without the minimum corpus being achieved. The FME now applies to extend it. The compliance officer should advise that:
option_a: The application is out of time, since extension must be sought while the PPM is valid
option_b: The extension is available on payment of 50% of the fresh-scheme filing fee
option_c: Multiple extensions are available at 25% and then 50% of the fresh-scheme fee
option_d: The extension is automatic, the memorandum reviving on payment of the prescribed fee

options.text: The application is out of time, since extension must be sought while the PPM is valid
The extension is available on payment of 50% of the fresh-scheme filing fee
Multiple extensions are available at 25% and then 50% of the fresh-scheme fee
The extension is automatic, the memorandum reviving on payment of the prescribed fee

explanation: The one-time six-month extension at 50% of the fresh-scheme fee exists, but it must be sought while the memorandum is still valid. Once it has lapsed there is nothing to extend. Note also that the multi-extension regime added in 2026 applies to restricted schemes, not SSFs.

title: An Authorised FME proposes an open-ended special situation fund that w
topic_name: Alternative Investment Funds – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: An Authorised FME proposes an open-ended special situation fund that will act as a resolution applicant under the IBC. The compliance officer should identify:
option_a: One defect — only the open-ended structure, since any FME may launch an SSF
option_b: Two defects — the FME category and the open-ended structure are both impermissible
option_c: One defect — only the FME category, since an SSF may be open- or close-ended
option_d: No defect — acting as a resolution applicant is expressly permitted for an SSF

options.text: One defect — only the open-ended structure, since any FME may launch an SSF
Two defects — the FME category and the open-ended structure are both impermissible
One defect — only the FME category, since an SSF may be open- or close-ended
No defect — acting as a resolution applicant is expressly permitted for an SSF

explanation: Acting as a resolution applicant is permitted (Reg. 54(2)), but an SSF may be launched only by a Registered FME and must be close-ended (Reg. 56(1)). Two independent defects — the permitted activity is a distraction from both.

title: What an SSF Invests In
topic_name: Alternative Investment Funds – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: A special situation fund is a scheme that invests in special situation assets and may additionally:
option_a: Act as a resolution applicant under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
option_b: Underwrite public issues of equity securities made by its investee companies
option_c: Provide bridge loans to its own fund management entity on arm's length terms
option_d: Act as an insolvency professional in proceedings before the Tribunal itself

options.text: Act as a resolution applicant under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
Underwrite public issues of equity securities made by its investee companies
Provide bridge loans to its own fund management entity on arm's length terms
Act as an insolvency professional in proceedings before the Tribunal itself

explanation: The SSF definition twins distressed-asset investing with eligibility to bid as a resolution applicant under the IBC — the regulatory bridge between IFSC capital and Indian insolvency resolution.

title: SSF Structure and Tenure
topic_name: Alternative Investment Funds – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: A special situation fund must be:
option_a: Open-ended only, with redemption available to investors at defined intervals throughout
option_b: Close-ended only, with a tenure of not less than three (3) years disclosed in the placement memorandum
option_c: Either open-ended or close-ended, at the option of the fund management entity concerned
option_d: Close-ended only, with a minimum tenure of five (5) years running from the first close

options.text: Open-ended only, with redemption available to investors at defined intervals throughout
Close-ended only, with a tenure of not less than three (3) years disclosed in the placement memorandum
Either open-ended or close-ended, at the option of the fund management entity concerned
Close-ended only, with a minimum tenure of five (5) years running from the first close

explanation: Reg. 56: close-ended only, minimum 3-year tenure. Distressed strategies need locked capital; redemption liquidity is structurally incompatible.

title: Who May Launch an SSF
topic_name: Alternative Investment Funds – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: A special situation fund may be launched by:
option_a: Only a Registered FME (Retail), through an offer document filed with the Authority
option_b: Any Authorised FME, provided that its net worth meets the prescribed minimum
option_c: A Registered FME, through a private placement memorandum filed with the Authority
option_d: Only banks and non-banking financial companies operating within the IFSC

options.text: Only a Registered FME (Retail), through an offer document filed with the Authority
Any Authorised FME, provided that its net worth meets the prescribed minimum
A Registered FME, through a private placement memorandum filed with the Authority
Only banks and non-banking financial companies operating within the IFSC

explanation: Reg. 55(1): Registered FMEs launch SSFs by private placement. Authorised FMEs — limited to VC schemes and FIFs — cannot.

title: SSF Filing Route
topic_name: Alternative Investment Funds – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: The filing of an SSF placement memorandum follows:
option_a: A 21-working-day prior review by the Authority, exactly as for retail schemes
option_b: A 30-working-day public comment process before any subscription may open at all
option_c: Case-by-case approval by the Authority before any subscription may be accepted
option_d: The green channel — open for subscription immediately upon taken-on-record communication

options.text: A 21-working-day prior review by the Authority, exactly as for retail schemes
A 30-working-day public comment process before any subscription may open at all
Case-by-case approval by the Authority before any subscription may be accepted
The green channel — open for subscription immediately upon taken-on-record communication

explanation: SSFs share the private-placement green channel: subscription opens on taken-on-record, with IFSCA retaining the right to comment at any stage for incorporation.

title: The SSF Extension — Still the Old Way
topic_name: Alternative Investment Funds – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: If an SSF misses its minimum corpus within PPM validity, the extension available is:
option_a: A one-time option to extend by 6 months, paying 50% of the fresh-scheme filing fee
option_b: Multiple six-month extensions at 25% and 50% fees, as for restricted schemes
option_c: No extension whatsoever; the placement memorandum simply lapses on expiry
option_d: An automatic twelve-month grace period requiring no further filing at all

options.text: A one-time option to extend by 6 months, paying 50% of the fresh-scheme filing fee
Multiple six-month extensions at 25% and 50% fees, as for restricted schemes
No extension whatsoever; the placement memorandum simply lapses on expiry
An automatic twelve-month grace period requiring no further filing at all

explanation: Reg. 55(3) was untouched by the 2026 Amendment: SSFs remain on the one-time, 6-month, 50%-fee regime while VC and restricted schemes moved to multi-extension. The asymmetry is deliberate exam bait.

title: Extending SSF Tenure Beyond Two Years
topic_name: Alternative Investment Funds – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: Extension of an SSF's tenure beyond the initial 2-year extension requires:
option_a: A fresh two-thirds vote of the investors by value at the end of each financial year
option_b: Express consent of willing investors, with an exit opportunity for dissenting investors
option_c: The approval of the Authority alone, without any reference to the investors
option_d: Nothing further, since extension beyond that point is prohibited absolutely

options.text: A fresh two-thirds vote of the investors by value at the end of each financial year
Express consent of willing investors, with an exit opportunity for dissenting investors
The approval of the Authority alone, without any reference to the investors
Nothing further, since extension beyond that point is prohibited absolutely

explanation: The ladder: up to 2 years on a 2/3-by-value vote; beyond that, only willing investors stay and dissenters must be offered an exit. Consent replaces majority coercion at the far end.

title: A retail scheme's offer document is filed 24 working days before launc
topic_name: Retail Schemes – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: A retail scheme's offer document is filed 24 working days before launch, with fiduciary approval scheduled for the following week. The compliance officer should identify that:
option_a: Nothing is defective, since 24 working days exceeds the 21-working-day requirement
option_b: The filing is premature, because fiduciary approval must precede the filing itself
option_c: The filing is defective only if the Authority's comments are not incorporated in time
option_d: The timeline should be 21 calendar days, so the filing is in fact earlier than required

options.text: Nothing is defective, since 24 working days exceeds the 21-working-day requirement
The filing is premature, because fiduciary approval must precede the filing itself
The filing is defective only if the Authority's comments are not incorporated in time
The timeline should be 21 calendar days, so the filing is in fact earlier than required

explanation: The 21-working-day timeline is met, but Reg. 43(5) bars filing a retail scheme at all until the fiduciaries have approved it. Sequence matters as much as timing — a compliant clock does not cure an out-of-order approval.

title: Six months after closure a retail scheme has 26 investors, the largest
topic_name: Retail Schemes – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: Six months after closure a retail scheme has 26 investors, the largest holding 28% of the corpus. The correct assessment is that the scheme:
option_a: Complies, because it exceeds the minimum of twenty investors within the cure period
option_b: Complies, because the 25% ceiling applies only at the time the offer closes
option_c: Breaches, because no single investor may exceed 25% once the cure period has expired

options.text: Complies, because it exceeds the minimum of twenty investors within the cure period
Complies, because the 25% ceiling applies only at the time the offer closes
Breaches, because no single investor may exceed 25% once the cure period has expired
Breaches, because a retail scheme requires at least fifty investors after six months

explanation: Reg. 44 imposes two conditions to be achieved within six months of closure: at least twenty investors AND no single investor above 25%. The investor count is satisfied; the concentration limit is not.

title: Investors holding 70% by value approve a two-year extension of a close
topic_name: Retail Schemes – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: Investors holding 70% by value approve a two-year extension of a close-ended retail scheme's tenure. The FME proceeds on that basis. The defect is that:

option_d: The approval of the Authority is also required, in addition to the investor vote

options.text: Two-thirds by value is insufficient; three-quarters approval is required for retail
Extension of a close-ended retail scheme's tenure is not permitted in any circumstances
The vote must be counted by number of investors rather than by value of holdings
The approval of the Authority is also required, in addition to the investor vote

explanation: Reg. 45(3) requires both two-thirds of investors by value AND the Authority's approval. The 70% vote satisfies the investor limb but not the regulatory one. Restricted schemes, by contrast, need only the investor resolution — a distinction worth holding.

title: Offer Document Filing Window
topic_name: Retail Schemes – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: A retail scheme's draft offer document must be filed with IFSCA at least:
option_a: Twenty-one (21) working days before the launch of the scheme

Fourteen (14) calendar days before the launch of the scheme
Thirty (30) working days before the launch of the scheme
Seven (7) working days before the launch of the scheme

explanation: Reg. 43(1): 21 working days, with applicable fees. Contrast with the private-placement green channel for VC/restricted schemes, where subscription can open immediately on taken-on-record.

title: Offer Document Validity
topic_name: Retail Schemes – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: The validity of a retail scheme's offer document is:
option_a: Six (6) months from the date the document is filed with IFSCA

Twelve (12) months from IFSCA's taken-on-record communication
Twenty-four (24) months from the launch date of the scheme
Perpetual, subject only to annual updation by the FME

explanation: Twelve months from taken-on-record — the same validity clock as VC and restricted scheme PPMs. The communication also serves as the Certificate of Registration for Income Tax Act purposes.

title: The 20/25 Rule
topic_name: Retail Schemes – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: A retail scheme must have:
option_a: At least 50 investors, with no single investor exceeding 10% of the corpus of the scheme at any time
option_b: At least 20 investors from the very first day of the offer, with no cure period at all

At least 20 investors from the very first day of the offer, with no cure period at all
At least 20 investors with no single investor exceeding 25%, achieved within 6 months of closure of the offer
At least 100 investors, with no concentration limit applying to any single investor

explanation: Reg. 44: minimum 20 investors, 25% single-investor cap, with a 6-month post-closure window to achieve compliance. The cure period is the detail exams isolate.

title: Legal Form of a Retail Scheme
topic_name: Retail Schemes – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: A retail scheme in IFSC must be constituted as:

Only a Trust settled under the Indian Trusts Act, 1882
Any form, including a variable capital company
A Company or a Trust under the applicable laws of India

explanation: Reg. 45(4): company or trust only. The LLP option — available for the FME entity itself and various restricted structures — is absent for retail schemes.

title: Extending a Close-Ended Retail Scheme
topic_name: Retail Schemes – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: The tenure of a close-ended retail scheme may be extended up to 2 years with:
option_a: Approval of two-thirds of investors by value AND the approval of the Authority
option_b: Approval of two-thirds of the investors by value, without any further approval

option_d: Approval of a simple majority of the investors counted by number, not value

Approval of two-thirds of the investors by value, without any further approval
Approval of the Authority alone, no investor resolution being required at all
Approval of a simple majority of the investors counted by number, not value

explanation: Reg. 45(3): retail extensions need both the 2/3-by-value investor vote and IFSCA approval — the extra Authority layer distinguishes retail from restricted/VC schemes, where investor approval suffices.

title: Fiduciary Approval of the Scheme
topic_name: Retail Schemes – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: A retail scheme may be filed with the Authority only if:

option_d: The scheme has secured anchor investors

It has been approved by the fiduciaries
IFSCA has pre-cleared the investment strategy
The scheme has secured anchor investors

explanation: Reg. 43(5): fiduciary approval (board of the scheme-company / trustees) is a precondition to filing itself. It cannot be ratified after the fact.

title: A Registered FME (Non-Retail) proposes an unlisted ETF marketed only t
topic_name: Retail Schemes – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: A Registered FME (Non-Retail) proposes an unlisted ETF marketed only to accredited investors. The compliance officer should identify that:
option_a: Only the listing is defective, since any Registered FME may launch an ETF

Only the category is defective, since accredited-investor ETFs need not be listed
Both the category and the listing are defective, whatever the investor profile
Neither is defective, provided the offer document discloses the absence of listing

explanation: Reg. 61(1) confines ETFs to a Registered FME (Retail), and Reg. 61(5) makes listing mandatory. Restricting the offer to accredited investors does not relax either requirement — investor sophistication is not a substitute for category or listing.

title: A Gold ETF holds 88% of AUM in physical gold and 9% in gold ETCDs, int
topic_name: Retail Schemes – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: A Gold ETF holds 88% of AUM in physical gold and 9% in gold ETCDs, intending to take physical delivery. The correct assessment is that:
option_a: Both limbs are satisfied, since ETCD exposure remains below the 10% ceiling

The ETCD position breaches the ceiling once the delivery intention is disclosed
Neither limb applies, because physical-delivery Gold ETFs are exempt from both
The 90% floor is breached, though the ETCD position is within its own limit

explanation: Reg. 65(1) requires at least 90% of AUM in gold and gold-related instruments; 88% falls short. The ETCD limb is satisfied, and the physical-delivery proviso relaxes the ETCD cap rather than the 90% floor.

title: Who May Launch an ETF
topic_name: Retail Schemes – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: Exchange Traded Funds in IFSC may be launched by:
option_a: Any Registered FME
option_b: Authorised FMEs with Authority approval
option_c: Recognised stock exchanges directly
option_d: Only Registered FMEs (Retail)

options.text: Any Registered FME
Authorised FMEs with Authority approval
Recognised stock exchanges directly
Only Registered FMEs (Retail)

explanation: Reg. 61(1): ETFs sit exclusively in the Retail tier — consistent with their public, exchange-traded nature. Filing follows the retail pattern: draft offer document 21 working days before launch.

title: ETF Filing and Validity
topic_name: Retail Schemes – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: The ETF offer document must be filed at least ____ before launch, with validity of ____:
option_a: 21 working days; 12 months from taken-on-record

30 working days; 6 months from the date of filing
14 working days; 12 months from the launch date
21 calendar days; 24 months from taken-on-record

explanation: Same discipline as retail schemes: 21-working-day prior filing, 12-month validity, comments incorporated pre-launch, material changes reported immediately.

title: The Listing Mandate
topic_name: Retail Schemes – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: An ETF launched in IFSC:
option_a: May be listed at the option of the fund management entity concerned
option_b: Must be mandatorily listed and traded on a recognised stock exchange

option_d: Trades exclusively over-the-counter between authorised participants

Must be mandatorily listed and traded on a recognised stock exchange
Must be listed only where its assets under management exceed USD 50 Million
Trades exclusively over-the-counter between authorised participants

explanation: Reg. 61(5): listing is mandatory — an unlisted ETF is a contradiction the regulations do not permit. The exchange itself becomes a second gatekeeper for novel ETF types.

title: The ETF Menu
topic_name: Retail Schemes – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: A "Hybrid ETF" under the regulations is one that:

option_d: Holds both physical and derivative gold

options.text: Combines active and passive strategies in one fund
Lists on two or more exchanges
Invests in two or more asset classes
Holds both physical and derivative gold

explanation: The permitted menu: Equity Index, Debt Index, Commodity-based, Hybrid (2+ asset classes), Actively Managed, and others subject to approval of the exchange and the Authority. Note that actively managed ETFs are expressly permitted.

title: Gold ETF Portfolio Test
topic_name: Retail Schemes – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: A Gold ETF must invest at least ____ of AUM in gold or bullion instruments, with ETCD exposure capped at ____:
option_d: 90%; 10% of AUM

explanation: Reg. 65(1): ≥90% in gold/bullion instruments (including Bullion Depository Receipts with gold underlying); gold-ETCD exposure ≤10% of AUM.

option_b: Stored with any scheduled commercial bank in India, and physically verified once each year by the fund management entity itself
option_c: Held by the FME itself at its own premises within the IFSC, and verified annually by its own statutory auditor

Held by the FME itself at its own premises within the IFSC, and verified annually by its own statutory auditor
Held with an overseas bullion bank of repute, and physically verified each quarter by the appointed custodian

explanation: Two safeguards: Authority-registered vault custody, plus independent half-yearly physical verification reported to the FME and fiduciaries within two months of each half-year.

90%, with silver-ETCD exposure not exceeding 10% of AUM
95%, with no exposure to silver-linked derivatives permitted
80%, with up to 20% held in gold for diversification purposes

explanation: Reg. 66(1) mirrors the gold architecture for silver: ≥90% in silver/bullion instruments (including BDRs with silver underlying), ETCD exposure ≤10%.

title: An Investment Trust raises funds privately from 45 investors, of whom
topic_name: Retail Schemes – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: An Investment Trust raises funds privately from 45 investors, of whom 40 invest USD 300,000 each and 5 are accredited investors investing USD 100,000 each. The position is that:
option_a: The placement is compliant on both the investor count and the investment thresholds
option_b: The placement is defective, because every investor must invest at least USD 250,000
option_c: The placement is defective, because accredited investors cannot be counted separately
option_d: The placement is compliant only if the five accredited investors are institutions

The placement is defective, because every investor must invest at least USD 250,000
The placement is defective, because accredited investors cannot be counted separately
The placement is compliant only if the five accredited investors are institutions

explanation: Reg. 93 permits investors investing at least USD 250,000 OR accredited investors, capped at fifty. Forty-five investors, with the smaller tickets coming from accredited investors, satisfies both limbs — the two categories are alternatives, not cumulative conditions.

title: For a public issue, an investment manager files the draft offer docume

question_text: For a public issue, an investment manager files the draft offer document 30 working days before the exchange filing, and the final offer document 3 working days before the offer opens. The defect is:

option_b: The final filing, which must be made not less than five working days before opening
option_c: Both filings, since the draft requires 45 working days and the final requires ten
option_d: Neither — both timelines comply with the requirements for a public issue

options.text: The draft filing, which must precede the exchange filing by 21 working days
The final filing, which must be made not less than five working days before opening
Both filings, since the draft requires 45 working days and the final requires ten
Neither — both timelines comply with the requirements for a public issue

explanation: The draft timeline of not less than thirty working days is met. The final offer document, however, must be filed not less than five working days before the offer opens (Reg. 94(g)); three is short.

title: Private Placement of an Investment Trust
topic_name: Retail Schemes – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: An Investment Trust (REIT/InvIT) raising funds by private placement must raise from:
option_a: Investors investing at least USD 250,000 or accredited investors, capped at fifty (50) investors
option_b: Any investors at all, subject only to an overall cap of two hundred (200) investors

option_d: Accredited investors only, with no cap at all on the number of such investors

options.text: Investors investing at least USD 250,000 or accredited investors, capped at fifty (50) investors
Any investors at all, subject only to an overall cap of two hundred (200) investors
Institutional investors only, subject to an overall cap of one thousand investors
Accredited investors only, with no cap at all on the number of such investors

explanation: Reg. 93: the private-placement gate is USD 250,000 / accredited status, with a 50-investor ceiling — the same sophistication thresholds as VC schemes.

title: Post-Allotment Filing
topic_name: Retail Schemes – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: After a private placement, the Investment Trust must file the final placement memorandum with the Authority within:
option_a: Five (5) working days from the closure of the placement

Ten (10) working days from the date of allotment of units
Thirty (30) days from the date of allotment of units
Before any allotment of units can lawfully occur

explanation: Reg. 93(d): final PM within 10 working days of allotment — a post-completion filing, unlike the pre-launch review that governs public issues.

title: Public Issue — Draft Offer Document Timing
topic_name: Retail Schemes – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: For a public issue, the Investment Trust (through its IM or investment banker) files the draft offer document:

option_d: Simultaneously with the filing that is made with the recognised stock exchange itself

Ten (10) working days before the issue opens for subscription by the investors concerned
Not less than thirty (30) working days before filing the offer document with the exchange and the Authority
Simultaneously with the filing that is made with the recognised stock exchange itself

explanation: Reg. 94(b): the 30-working-day runway precedes the formal offer document filing — creating space for the public comment and observation process.

title: Public Comments Window

options.text: Seven (7) days, on the website of the Authority alone and on no other website
Twenty-one (21) working days, on the website of the recognised stock exchange only
Thirty (30) days, by advertisement published in two national daily newspapers
Not less than fourteen (14) days, on the websites of the Authority, exchange(s), investment manager and bankers

explanation: Reg. 94(c): a minimum 14-day public exposure across four sets of websites — the crowdsourced layer of due diligence unique to public offers.

title: The Due Diligence Certificate
topic_name: Retail Schemes – Concepts, Structures & Framework
question_text: The draft offer document and offer document must be accompanied by a due diligence certificate signed by:
option_a: The investment manager or the investment banker, as the case may be

The trustees of the Investment Trust, acting on behalf of unit holders
The statutory auditor of the Investment Trust for the relevant year
The board of directors of the sponsor of the Investment Trust

title: A Registered FME (Non-Retail) is asked to act as investment manager fo
topic_name: Regulatory Framework for Fund Management in IFSC
question_text: A Registered FME (Non-Retail) is asked to act as investment manager for a REIT proposing a public offer. Which statement is MOST accurate?

option_b: It may act, since a Non-Retail FME is permitted to manage REITs and InvITs generally

title: A Registered FME (Non-Retail) met USD 500,000 net worth at registratio

question_text: A Registered FME (Non-Retail) met USD 500,000 net worth at registration. Eighteen months later accumulated losses reduce it to USD 460,000. What should the compliance officer identify first?

options.text: That net worth is an entry condition, tested only at the time of registration
That net worth must be maintained at all times, so the FME is currently in breach
That the shortfall is acceptable while the FME remains profitable on a cash basis
That the FME may continue provided it restores the shortfall before the year end

title: A branch FME's parent holds net worth far above the prescribed minimum

question_text: A branch FME's parent holds net worth far above the prescribed minimum, but none of it is earmarked for the IFSC branch. What is the position?
option_a: Compliant, because the requirement attaches to the parent's total net worth
option_b: Compliant, provided the parent furnishes an annual solvency certificate

options.text: Compliant, because the requirement attaches to the parent's total net worth
Compliant, provided the parent furnishes an annual solvency certificate
Not compliant, because the amount must be earmarked for the branch in the IFSC
Not compliant, because a branch must hold the net worth within the IFSC itself

explanation: Reg. 8(2) permits the minimum net worth to sit at parent level, but its proviso requires that amount to be EARMARKED for the IFSC branch. Holding a large balance sheet generally is not enough; equally, the regulation does not require the funds to be held inside the IFSC.

title: Which activity can an Authorised FME undertake WITHOUT moving to a hig

option_a: Offering Portfolio Management Services to accredited investors

option_c: Acting as investment manager for a private placement of an InvIT
option_d: Managing a Family Investment Fund established for a Single Family

Launching a restricted scheme open to accredited investors
Acting as investment manager for a private placement of an InvIT
Managing a Family Investment Fund established for a Single Family

title: An Authorised FME intends to begin offering Portfolio Management Servi

option_b: Launch exchange traded funds and retail schemes, and act as investment manager for private placements of REITs and InvITs

title: A candidate KMP holds a professional qualification and four years' rel
topic_name: Regulatory Framework for Fund Management in IFSC
question_text: A candidate KMP holds a professional qualification and four years' relevant experience. For a role under sub-regulation (2), the compliance officer should conclude that the candidate:

Falls short, because the base requirement of five years applies to every KMP role

Falls short, because professional qualifications count only towards the certification route

explanation: The first proviso to Reg. 7(5)(b) reduces the requirement to three years where the KMP holds a professional qualification. Four years therefore suffices. The five-year figure is the base rule, and the certification route is a separate alternative rather than an additional condition.

title: An FME registered in the IFSC also carries on a separate regulated act

title: The Principal Officer's Mandate

question_text: The Principal Officer of an FME carries overall responsibility for:

title: Who Is the Additional KMP?

Compliance Officer

explanation: Reg. 7(2): the second mandatory KMP is the Compliance Officer, responsible for regulatory compliance and implementation of risk management policies. "Compliance and Risk Manager" is the superseded 2022 designation.

explanation: Reg. 7(3): the fund-management KMP must be in place before the first retail scheme or ETF offer document is filed — a pre-filing gate, not a post-launch obligation.

explanation: The trap: the January 2026 Amendment rewrote the extension regime for VC schemes (Reg. 19) and restricted schemes (Reg. 35), but did NOT touch Reg. 55(3) for Special Situation Funds. SSFs remain on the old one-time, 6-month, 50%-fee regime. Asymmetries created by amendments are prime examination territory.

title: New Winding-Up Ground
topic_name: Regulatory Framework for Fund Management in IFSC
question_text: The January 2026 Amendment inserted a new ground for winding up a scheme. It applies where:
option_a: The FME raised funds but missed the minimum corpus within the (extended) PPM validity, and did not extend that validity by filing and paying the fee
option_b: The Authority, acting suo motu, determines that the scheme has become unviable and directs that it be wound up
option_c: Investors holding fifty per cent of the value of the scheme pass a resolution requiring it to be wound up
option_d: The net asset value of the scheme falls fifty per cent below par and the FME cannot restore it that year

options.text: The FME raised funds but missed the minimum corpus within the (extended) PPM validity, and did not extend that validity by filing and paying the fee
The Authority, acting suo motu, determines that the scheme has become unviable and directs that it be wound up
Investors holding fifty per cent of the value of the scheme pass a resolution requiring it to be wound up

explanation: New Reg. 131(1)(c): an exit route where a scheme raised some money, never hit minimum corpus within validity, and the FME has not filed (with fee) for a further extension. The 2026 Amendment ALSO inserted Reg. 131(1)(d): winding up where no investors were onboarded and no funds collected, and the FME voluntarily desires to wind up. The 75%-by-value investor resolution under Reg. 131(1)(b) remains separate again.

title: A close-ended restricted scheme resolves, by 80% of investors by value

option_a: The change is effective, since the investor threshold of 75% by value is exceeded
option_b: The change requires the Authority's prior approval in addition to the investor vote
option_c: The change cannot take effect yet, because the amendment has not been notified
option_d: The change is effective only for schemes whose corpus exceeds USD 3 Million

options.text: The change is effective, since the investor threshold of 75% by value is exceeded
The change requires the Authority's prior approval in addition to the investor vote
The change cannot take effect yet, because the amendment has not been notified
The change is effective only for schemes whose corpus exceeds USD 3 Million

explanation: Even though the 75%-by-value condition attaching to the approved change is satisfied, the amendment has not been notified. Until it is, the existing NAV requirement governs. Approval sets direction; notification creates the obligation.

title: The Ceiling That Isn’t Law Yet
topic_name: Regulatory Framework for Fund Management in IFSC
question_text: Today, an FME's contribution to its own VC scheme is capped at what share of targeted corpus?
option_a: 25%, effective from the date of the Authority meeting held on 24 July 2026
option_b: 2.5%, which operates as both the floor and the ceiling for such schemes
option_c: There is no ceiling at all on an FME's contribution to a VC scheme
option_d: 10% — the notified ceiling under Reg. 28(1); the approved 25% is not yet notified

options.text: 25%, effective from the date of the Authority meeting held on 24 July 2026
2.5%, which operates as both the floor and the ceiling for such schemes
There is no ceiling at all on an FME's contribution to a VC scheme
10% — the notified ceiling under Reg. 28(1); the approved 25% is not yet notified

explanation: Reg. 28(1) caps the contribution at 10% of targeted corpus, and that is what binds until the amendment is notified. Two separate things are easily confused: (i) the ALREADY-notified carve-out disapplying the 10% ceiling where the FME and its associates are resident outside India with no Indian UBO and not more than one-third of corpus goes to one investee; and (ii) the APPROVED 25% ceiling for FMEs with Indian UBOs investing only in IFSC/foreign jurisdictions. 2.5% is the floor, not the ceiling.
